dispositions.method: The automatic families first printed in 1802 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 1,378 items printed somewhere; 85 in 7 or more papers by the finder's count, 16 in 9 or more). Because the Treasury report, the proclamations of December 1801 and the acts of the session sit in families that began in 1801, the same script was also run with year 1801 over the 1802 pages (items_from_1801.json: 171 items, 19 in 7 or more). The finder's counts are those of chains (it joins items printed together, and acts that share the enacting formula), so every item in 6 or more papers was read in this session (Claude, the session's own model; no second reader) and counted by its own words, and every item in 5 or more was checked by machine for further papers: about 220 words of its text were compared with every page of the year in both transcriptions, and every page that shared many of its word sequences was read. Each act of the session was counted by its own title followed by its enacting clause. Each chosen item and each candidate set aside was counted with phrase searches on all 2,968 pages of 1802 in both transcriptions (story_phrase_search.py, phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json); every hit was read.
dispositions.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1800, 1804, 1805, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests; items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months from January to December and the main kinds of news (Europe and St. Domingo; ships, trade and the Barbary states; American public life and government). Where several items of one affair reach the band in the same weeks, the most widely printed was chosen and the others were not, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01); the Barbary items were trimmed as in 1804 and 1805. Every story alike (the owner's rule of 11 November 2026): no item was left out for its subject. Where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story. A group count is a target, not a quota.
dispositions.paper_counting: Papers, not catalogue numbers, are counted (C-04): Jenks's Portland Gazette (sn83016063 to 20 September, sn83016072 from 27 September: Number 230 and 231 of Volume V), the Recorder of Richmond (sn84024678 to 27 October, sn84024679 from 3 November: the same printers, Pace and Callender) and E. Russell's paper at Concord, New Hampshire (sn84022876, the Republican Gazette, to 3 August; sn90062293, the American Republican Gazette, from 10 August) are one paper each. The 14 catalogue series of 1802 are 11 papers.

counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of the first session of the Seventh Congress through their enacting formula and the list of acts (items of up to 9 papers and 96 printings). Counted by its own title followed by its enacting clause, no act reaches 9 papers and three reach 7: the act fixing the military peace establishment (admitted), the act for the apportionment of Representatives and the act establishing a uniform rule of naturalization (not chosen). Five papers printed nearly every law (the National Intelligencer, Kentucky Gazette, New Hampshire Gazette, Rhode-Island Republican and Republican Ledger); the Oracle, the Portland Gazette, the Alexandria Advertiser and the Virginia Argus printed some. Pages that mention an act in the proceedings, or recite it in another act, are not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Thomas Paine's letters to the citizens: The finder makes items of single paragraphs of Paine's letters (up to 10 papers). Each letter is counted by its opening (C-06): the first letter is in 9 papers (the American Republican Gazette's printing of 7 December has its opening in print and in the CA text; RevX leaves it out), the second in 8, the third in 6 and the fourth in 6. Pages that quote passages in commentary are not counted (C-07): the Recorder's comments of 1 and 8 December, and the Alexandria Advertiser's reprint of them; the Kentucky Gazette's quotation of the first letter's last paragraph on 30 November; the Recorder's 'Extract from Paine's second letter' of 15 December; the Portland Gazette's quotations of the second and third letters. The passage on a 'female literary correspondent' that the first letter quotes also stands in Paine's letter to George Washington of 1796, which the Alexandria Advertiser reprinted in November; it is not counted with the first letter.
counted_item_by_item.The President's letter to Thomas Paine: Counted by its opening: 8 papers. A page that prints the letter whole counts, even inside an essay or among other letters, and the Alexandria Advertiser (12 October) and the Portland Gazette (6 December) printed it a second time (C-08); pages that quote part of it do not count (C-07): the Rhode-Island Republican's essay 'Seventy-Five, No. VI' of 25 September quotes only its first sentence, and the Alexandria Advertiser (16 October) and the Oracle (20 November) quote it from its second sentence.
counted_item_by_item.The committee's report on the public mon: The report of the House committee appointed 'to enquire and report whether monies drawn from the Treasury have been faithfully applied' (April 1802) is chained by the finder into items of 9 papers. By its opening it is in 6 papers (National Intelligencer, Alexandria Advertiser, Republican Ledger, Kentucky Gazette, Republican Gazette, Oracle); the Recorder and the Rhode-Island Republican printed extracts from its later parts, which are not counted (C-06); the Virginia Argus and the National Intelligencer's 'History of the last session' summarise it (C-07).
counted_item_by_item.The Treasury report of December 1801: The Secretary of the Treasury's report of 18 December 1801 on the finances was printed in parts in January 1802; the finder makes items of its paragraphs. By its opening it is in 7 papers on 1802 pages (the National Intelligencer printed it in December 1801). Later pages that quote its figures (the National Intelligencer and the Virginia Argus in August and September) are not counted. The page of the National Intelligencer filed under 29 November that opens with the same formula is the issue of 29 December 1802 and prints the next year's report.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: One item in two wordings or translations counts as one (C-02): the Consuls' proclamation to the inhabitants of St. Domingo (4 and 3 papers: 'you are all Frenchmen ... But an entire change has taken place', and 'ye are all Frenchmen, ye are all free ... But all is changed'), General Leclerc's proclamation of 8 June (6 and 3), the French Senate's address to the First Consul for life (5 and 3), the New York report of the fire of 2 November (5 and 2), and the New York report of the Algerine cruisers (7, and the Virginia Argus's Philadelphia form, which opens in other words and goes on in the same).

for_user_decision.Thomas Paine's first letter admitted wit: As built, the first letter is in 9 papers because the American Republican Gazette of 7 December has its opening in print (RevX leaves it out); without that page it is in 8 and would still be chosen as a sub-story under the Paine parent.
for_user_decision.General Leclerc's proclamation of June 1: As built, admitted by the rule's first part with its two translations counted together (6 + 3, C-02), as 1800 counted the convention with France; counted apart, the longer translation is in 6 papers.
for_user_decision.The President's letter to Paine counted: As built, a page that prints the letter whole counts, even inside an essay or a column of other letters (two papers printed it twice); pages that quote part of it do not. The paper count, 8, is the same either way.
for_user_decision.Paine's letters admitted in his own word: As built, the first two letters are shown with excerpts of their openings and described as Paine's political argument; the second makes allegations against John Adams by name, labelled as allegations in the description.
for_user_decision.St. Domingo in four groups: As built, St. Domingo has four groups in three stories (the report of Toussaint's death in January, the Consuls' proclamation and the burning of the Cape in March, Leclerc's proclamation on Toussaint's arrest in June), each described by whose account it is in the papers' words; the report of January is a rumour, as the Baltimore paper itself says. The Consuls' proclamation reaches 7 papers with its two translations counted together (4 + 3); it stands under its parent either way (C-01).
for_user_decision.The Barbary items trimmed: As built, two Barbary stories (the Algerine cruisers' capture of a Portuguese frigate, the letters from Algiers of 7 July); four items in 7 papers are not chosen (the Dey of Tripoli's frigate, the Morocco rebellion, the frigate New York, Mr. Simpson's dispatches).
for_user_decision.Misdated issues of the National Intellig: Several issues of the National Intelligencer of 1802 are filed under other dates (see the README, 'Data issues'). As built, its printed date is the filed one until a correction release dates the issue as printed.
